entries.translation: De Arquímedes, aunque sus hallazgos fueron muchos, admirables y variados, de todos ellos el que voy a exponer parece haber sido concebido con una sagacidad infinita. En efecto, Hierón, engrandecido en Siracusa con el poder regio, habiendo decidido, tras el éxito de sus empresas, colocar en cierto santuario una corona de oro votiva a los dioses inmortales, contrató su hechura por un precio de mano de obra y pesó el oro para el contratista con una balanza. Este, a su tiempo, presentó al rey la obra, hecha finamente a mano, y en la balanza pareció haber cumplido con el peso de la corona.

entries.latin: Posteaquam indicium est factum dempto auro tantundem argenti in id coronarium opus admixtum esse, indignatus Hiero se contemptum esse neque inveniens, qua ratione id furtum reprehenderet, rogavit Archimeden, uti in se sumeret sibi de eo cogitationem. Tunc is, cum haberet eius rei curam, casu venit in balineum, ibique cum in solium descenderet, animadvertit, quantum corporis sui in eo insideret, tantum aquae extra solium effluere. Idque cum eius rei rationem explicationis ostendisset, non est moratus, sed exsiluit gaudio motus de solio et nudus vadens domum ⟨uni⟩versis significabat clara voce invenisse, quod quaereret; nam currens identidem graece clamabat εὕρηκα εὕρηκα.
entries.translation: Después de que se hizo la denuncia de que, sustraído oro, se había mezclado en esa obra de la corona una cantidad igual de plata, Hierón, indignado por haber sido burlado y no encontrando el procedimiento con que probar ese hurto, rogó a Arquímedes que tomara sobre sí la reflexión acerca de ello. Entonces este, ocupado en el asunto, fue por azar a los baños, y allí, al descender a la bañera, advirtió que cuanto de su cuerpo se sumergía en ella, tanta agua salía fuera de la bañera. Y como esto le mostró el principio de la solución del asunto, no se demoró, sino que saltó, movido por la alegría, de la bañera y, yendo desnudo a su casa, anunciaba a todos en voz alta que había encontrado lo que buscaba; pues, corriendo, gritaba una y otra vez en griego: εὕρηκα, εὕρηκα.

entries.latin: Tum vero ex eo inventionis ingressu duas fecisse dicitur massas aequo pondere, quo etiam fuerat corona, unam ex auro et alteram ex argento. Cum ita fecisset, vas amplum ad summa labra implevit aquae, in quo demisit argenteam massam. Cuius quanta magnitudo in vasum depressa est, tantum aquae effluxit. Ita exempta massa quanto minus factum fuerat, refudit sextario mensus, ut eodem modo, quo prius fuerat, ad labra aequaretur. Ita ex eo invenit, quantum pondus argenti ad certam aquae mensuram responderet.
entries.translation: Entonces, a partir de ese principio de su hallazgo, se dice que hizo dos masas del mismo peso que tenía la corona, una de oro y otra de plata. Hecho esto, llenó de agua hasta el borde un recipiente amplio, en el que sumergió la masa de plata. Cuanto volumen de ella se hundió en el recipiente, tanta agua se derramó. Así, sacada la masa, volvió a verter, midiéndolo con un sextario, lo que había disminuido, para que el agua se igualara hasta el borde del mismo modo que estaba antes. Así halló qué peso de plata respondía a una medida determinada de agua.

entries.latin: Cum id expertus esset, tum auream massam similiter pleno vaso demisit et ea exempta, eadem ratione mensura addita invenit ex aquae numero sextantum minore, quanto minus magno corpore eodem pondere auri massa esset quam argenti. Postea vero repleto vaso in eadem aqua ipsa corona demissa invenit plus aquae defluxisse in corona quam in aurea eodem pondere massa, et ita ex eo, quod fuerat plus aquae in corona quam in massa, ratiocinatus reprehendit argenti in auro mixtionem et manifestum furtum redemptoris.
entries.translation: Hecha esta prueba, sumergió del mismo modo la masa de oro en el recipiente lleno y, sacada esta, añadiendo la medida por el mismo procedimiento, halló, por la menor cantidad de sextarios de agua, cuánto menor en volumen era la masa de oro que la de plata del mismo peso. Después, llenado de nuevo el recipiente y sumergida en la misma agua la corona misma, halló que se había derramado más agua con la corona que con la masa de oro del mismo peso; y así, razonando a partir de que había habido más agua con la corona que con la masa, probó la mezcla de plata en el oro y el hurto manifiesto del contratista.

entries.latin: Transferatur mens ad Archytae Tarentini et Eratosthenis Cyrenaei cogitata; hi enim multa et grata a mathematicis rebus hominibus invenerunt. Itaque cum in ceteris inventionibus fuerint grati, in eius rei cogitationibus maxime sunt suspecti. Alius enim alia ratione explicaverunt, quod Delo imperaverat responsis Apollo, uti arae eius, quantum haberent pedum quadratorum, id duplicarentur, et ita fore uti, qui essent in ea insula, tunc religione liberarentur.
entries.translation: Pásese ahora la atención a los pensamientos de Arquitas de Tarento y de Eratóstenes de Cirene; pues estos hallaron para los hombres muchas cosas gratas a partir de las matemáticas. Y así, aunque hayan sido gratos en sus demás hallazgos, en sus reflexiones sobre este asunto son sobre todo admirados. Pues explicaron cada uno por un procedimiento distinto lo que Apolo había ordenado en Delos mediante sus oráculos: que se duplicara el número de pies cúbicos que tenía su altar, y que así sucedería que quienes vivían en esa isla quedarían entonces libres de la culpa religiosa.

entries.latin: Itaque Archytas cylindrorum descriptionibus, Eratosthenes organica mesolabi ratione idem explicaverunt. Cum haec sint tam magnis doctrinarum iucunditatibus animadversa et cogamur naturaliter inventionibus singularum rerum considerantes effectus moveri, multas res attendens admiror etiam Democriti de rerum natura volumina et eius commentarium, quod inscribitur Χειροκμήτων, †in quo etiam utebatur anulo signaretur amolcie est expertus.
entries.translation: Así, Arquitas con el trazado de cilindros y Eratóstenes con el procedimiento instrumental del mesolabio explicaron lo mismo. Puesto que estas cosas se han advertido con tan grandes deleites de las doctrinas, y nos vemos naturalmente obligados a conmovernos al considerar los efectos de los hallazgos de cada cosa, atendiendo a muchas cosas, admiro también los volúmenes de Demócrito sobre la naturaleza de las cosas y su tratado que se titula Χειρόκμητα, †en el que también se servía de un anillo para sellar con cera blanda lo que había experimentado†.

entries.latin: Ergo eorum virorum cogitata non solum ad mores corrigendos, sed etiam ad omnium utilitatem perpetuo sunt praeparata, athletarum autem nobilitates brevi spatio cum suis corporibus senescunt. Itaque neque cum maxime sunt florentes neque posteritati hi, quemadmodum sapientium cogitata hominum vitae, prodesse possunt.
entries.translation: Así pues, los pensamientos de estos hombres están preparados perpetuamente no solo para corregir las costumbres, sino también para la utilidad de todos; en cambio, la celebridad de los atletas envejece en breve espacio junto con sus cuerpos. Así, ni cuando están en su mayor florecimiento ni para la posteridad pueden estos ser útiles a la vida de los hombres, como lo son los pensamientos de los sabios.

entries.latin: Cum vero neque moribus neque institutis scriptorum praestantibus tribuantur honores, ipsae [autem] per se mentes aeris altiora prospicientes memoriarum gradibus ad caelum elatae aevo inmortali non modo sententias sed etiam figuras eorum posteris cogunt esse notas. Itaque, qui litterarum iucunditatibus instinctas habent mentes, non possunt non in suis pectoribus dedicatum habere, sicuti deorum, sic Ennii poetae simulacrum; Accii autem carminibus qui studiose delectantur, non modo verborum virtutes sed etiam figuram eius videntur secum habere praesentem [esse].
entries.translation: Y, aunque no se tributen honores a las costumbres ni a las enseñanzas sobresalientes de los escritores, las mentes mismas, mirando por sí solas a lo más alto del aire, elevadas al cielo por los grados de la memoria, obligan con su eternidad inmortal a que sean conocidos por la posteridad no solo sus pensamientos, sino también sus figuras. Así, quienes tienen las mentes inspiradas por los deleites de las letras no pueden dejar de tener consagrada en sus pechos, como la de los dioses, la imagen del poeta Ennio; y quienes se deleitan con afán en los versos de Accio parecen tener presente consigo no solo la virtud de sus palabras, sino también su figura.

entries.latin: Item plures post nostram memoriam nascentes cum Lucretio videbuntur velut coram de rerum natura disputare, de arte vero rhetorica cum Cicerone, multi posterorum cum Varrone conferent sermonem de lingua latina, non minus etiam plures philologi cum Graecorum sapientibus multa deliberantes secretos cum his videbuntur habere sermones, et ad summam sapientium scriptorum sententiae corporibus absentibus vetustate florentes cum insunt inter consilia et disputationes, maiores habent, quam praesentium sunt, auctoritates omnes.
entries.translation: Igualmente, muchos que nazcan después de nuestro tiempo parecerán disputar como en persona con Lucrecio sobre la naturaleza de las cosas, y sobre el arte retórica con Cicerón; muchos de los venideros conversarán con Varrón sobre la lengua latina; y no menos, muchos filólogos, deliberando muchas cosas con los sabios de los griegos, parecerán tener con ellos conversaciones reservadas; y, en suma, las sentencias de los escritores sabios, florecientes con el tiempo aunque sus cuerpos estén ausentes, cuando intervienen en los consejos y en las disputas, tienen todas mayor autoridad que las de los presentes.

entries.latin: Itaque, Caesar, his auctoribus fretus sensibus eorum adhibitis et consiliis ea volumina conscripsi, et prioribus septem de aedificiis, octavo de aquis, in hoc de gnomonicis rationibus, quemadmodum de radiis solis in mundo sunt per umbras gnomonis inventae quibusque rationibus dilatentur aut contrahantur, explicabo.
entries.translation: Por eso, César, confiado en estos autores, aplicando sus sentidos y sus consejos, he escrito estos volúmenes: en los siete primeros, sobre los edificios; en el octavo, sobre las aguas; en este explicaré los principios de la gnomónica, cómo se han hallado a partir de los rayos del sol en el mundo mediante las sombras del gnomon, y con qué procedimientos se alargan o se acortan.

entries.latin: Nobili Graecorum et ampla civitate Ephesi lex vetusta dicitur a maioribus dura condicione sed iure esse non iniquo constituta. Nam architectus, cum publicum opus curandum recipit, pollicetur, quanto sumptu id sit futurum. Tradita aestimatione magistratui bona eius obligantur, donec opus sit perfectum. Absoluto autem, cum ad dictum inpensa respondit, decretis et honoribus ornatur. Item si non amplius quam quarta ad aestimationem est adicienda, de publico praestatur, neque ulla poena tenetur. Cum vero amplius quam quarta in opere consumitur, ex eius bonis ad perficiendum pecunia exigitur.
entries.translation: En la noble y grande ciudad griega de Éfeso se dice que los antepasados establecieron una antigua ley, de condición dura, pero de derecho no injusto. En efecto, el arquitecto, cuando se hace cargo de una obra pública, promete cuál será su coste. Entregada la estimación al magistrado, sus bienes quedan obligados hasta que la obra esté terminada. Y, concluida esta, si el gasto responde a lo dicho, se le honra con decretos y honores. Asimismo, si no hay que añadir más de una cuarta parte a la estimación, se paga del erario público y no queda sujeto a pena alguna. Pero cuando en la obra se gasta más de una cuarta parte, se exige de sus bienes el dinero para terminarla.

entries.latin: Utinam dii inmortales fecissent, ea lex etiam P. R. non modo publicis sed etiam privatis aedificiis esset constituta! Namque non sine poena grassarentur inperiti, sed qui summa doctrinarum subtilitate essent prudentes, sine dubitatione profiterentur architecturam, neque patres familiarum inducerentur ad infinitas sumptuum profusiones, ut et e bonis eicerentur, ipsique architecti poenae timore coacti diligentius modum inpensarum ratiocinantes explicarent, uti patres familiarum ad id, quod praeparavissent, seu paulo amplius adicientes, aedificia expedirent. Nam qui quadringenta ad opus possunt parare, si adicient centum, habendo spem perfectionis delectationibus tenentur; qui autem adiectione dimidia aut ampliore sumptu onerantur, amissa spe et inpensa abiecta, fractis rebus et animis desistere coguntur.
entries.translation: ¡Ojalá los dioses inmortales hubieran hecho que esa ley se estableciera también para el pueblo romano, no solo para los edificios públicos, sino también para los privados! Pues los inexpertos no causarían estragos sin castigo, sino que profesarían sin vacilación la arquitectura quienes fueran prudentes por la suma sutileza de su doctrina; y los padres de familia no serían inducidos a infinitos derroches de gastos, hasta el punto de verse despojados de sus bienes, y los propios arquitectos, obligados por el temor al castigo, calcularían y fijarían con más diligencia la medida de los gastos, de modo que los padres de familia terminaran sus edificios con lo que hubieran preparado o añadiendo un poco más. Pues quienes pueden reunir cuatrocientos para una obra, si añaden cien, conservando la esperanza de terminarla, se mantienen en su deleite; pero quienes se ven cargados con un aumento de la mitad o con un gasto mayor, perdida la esperanza y abandonado el gasto, arruinados en sus bienes y en sus ánimos, se ven obligados a desistir.

entries.latin: Nec solum id vitium in aedificiis, sed etiam in muneribus, quae a magistratibus foro gladiatorum scaenisque ludorum dantur, quibus nec mora neque expectatio conceditur, sed necessitas finito tempore perficere cogit, id est sedes spectaculorum velorumque inductiones et ea omnia, quae scaenicis moribus per machinationem ad spectationes populo comparantur. In his vero opus est prudentia diligens et ingenii doctissimi cogitata, quod nihil eorum perficitur sine machinatione studiorumque vario ac sollerti vigore.
entries.translation: Y este defecto no se da solo en los edificios, sino también en los espectáculos que los magistrados ofrecen en el foro, de gladiadores, y en las escenas de los juegos, para los cuales no se concede ni demora ni espera, sino que la necesidad obliga a terminarlos en un tiempo fijado, es decir, los asientos de los espectáculos, el despliegue de los toldos y todo lo que, según las costumbres escénicas, se prepara mediante maquinaria para que el pueblo lo contemple. En estas cosas se necesita, ciertamente, una prudencia diligente y los pensamientos de un ingenio doctísimo, porque ninguna de ellas se lleva a cabo sin maquinaria y sin el vigor variado y sagaz de los estudios.

entries.latin: Igitur quoniam haec ita sunt tradita et constituta, non videtur esse alienum, uti caute summaque diligentia, antequam instituantur opera, eorum expediantur rationes. Ergo quoniam neque lex neque morum institutio id potest cogere et quotannis et praetores et aediles ludorum causa machinationes praeparare debent, visum mihi est, imperator, non esse alienum, quoniam de aedificiis in prioribus voluminibus exposui, in hoc, quod finitionem summam corporis habet constitutam, quae sint principia machinarum, ordinata praeceptis explicare.
entries.translation: Así pues, puesto que estas cosas se han transmitido y establecido así, no parece ajeno que, con cautela y suma diligencia, antes de emprender las obras, se desarrollen sus principios. Por tanto, puesto que ni la ley ni la institución de las costumbres pueden obligar a ello, y cada año tanto los pretores como los ediles deben preparar maquinarias para los juegos, me ha parecido, emperador, no ajeno, puesto que en los volúmenes anteriores he expuesto lo relativo a los edificios, explicar en este, que contiene la conclusión suprema del cuerpo, cuáles son los principios de las máquinas, ordenados en preceptos.

entries.latin: Cum divina tua mens et numen, imperator Caesar, imperio potiretur orbis terrarum invictaque virtute cunctis hostibus stratis, triumpho victoriaque tua cives gloriarentur et gentes omnes subactae tuum spectarent nutum populusque Romanus et senatus liberatus timore amplissimis tuis cogitationibus consiliisque gubernaretur, non audebam, tantis occupationibus, de architectura scripta et magnis cogitationibus explicata edere, metuens ne non apto tempore interpellans subirem tui animi offensionem.
entries.translation: While your divine mind and inspiration, Emperor Caesar, held dominion over the world, and, once all enemies had been vanquished by your invincible valour, the citizens rejoiced in your triumph and victory, all subjugated nations awaited your signal, and the Roman people and the Senate, freed from fear, were guided by your profound reflections and counsel, I dared not, amidst such lofty occupations, publish my writings on architecture, composed after extensive meditations, fearing that, by interrupting you at an inopportune moment, I might incur your displeasure.

entries.latin: Cum vero attenderem te non solum de vita communi omnium curam publicaeque rei constitutione habere, sed etiam de opportunitate publicorum aedificiorum, ut civitas per te non solum provinciis esset aucta, verum etiam ut maiestas imperii publicorum aedificiorum egregias haberet auctoritates, non putavi praetermittendum quin primo quoque tempore de his rebus ea tibi ederem, ideo quod primum parenti tuo de eo fueram notus et eius virtutis studiosus. Cum autem concilium caelestium in sedibus inmortalitatis eum dedicavisset et imperium parentis in tuam potestatem transtulisset, idem studium meum in eius memoria permanens in te contulit favorem. Itaque cum M. Aurelio et P. Minidio et Gn. Cornelio ad apparationem ballistarum et scorpionum reliquorumque tormentorum refectionem fui praesto et cum eis commoda accepi, quae cum primo mihi tribuisti, recognitionem per sororis commendationem servasti.
entries.translation: But when I observed that you were not only concerned with the common life of all and with the ordering of the commonwealth, but also with the fitness of public buildings—so that the State was enlarged not only by your provinces, but also that the majesty of the empire might possess the eminent authority of its public buildings—I did not think it right to omit laying these matters before you at the earliest opportunity, the more so because I had first been known to your father and was an admirer of his virtue. But when the council of the heavenly powers had consecrated him among the seats of immortality and had transferred your father's empire into your power, that same devotion of mine, abiding in his memory, transferred my allegiance to you. And so, together with Marcus Aurelius, Publius Minidius and Gnaeus Cornelius, I was at hand for the preparation of ballistae and scorpiones and the repair of the other engines of war, and with them I received my emoluments, which, once you had first granted them to me, you continued to me by your sister's recommendation.

entries.latin: Cum ergo eo beneficio essem obligatus, ut ad exitum vitae non haberem inopiae timorem, haec tibi scribere coepi, quod animadverti multa te aedificavisse et nunc aedificare, reliquo quoque tempore et publicorum et privatorum aedificiorum, pro amplitudine rerum gestarum ut posteris memoriae traderentur, curam habiturum. Conscripsi praescriptiones terminatas, ut eas attendens et ante facta et futura qualia sint opera per te posses nota habere; namque his voluminibus aperui omnes disciplinae rationes.
entries.translation: Since this favor bound me to you and freed me from the fear of poverty for the rest of my life, I began to write these books for you. I had observed that you had built many works and were still building, and that you would continue to care for public and private buildings on a scale commensurate with your achievements, so that they might be handed down to posterity. I have set down precise rules so that, by attending to them, you may judge for yourself the quality of works already completed and of those yet to come; for in these volumes I have explained all the principles of the discipline.

entries.latin: Dinocrates architectus cogitationibus et sollertia fretus, cum Alexander rerum potiretur, profectus est e Macedonia ad exercitum regiae cupidus commendationis. Is e patria a propinquis et amicis tulit ad primos ordines et purpuratos litteras ut aditus haberet faciliores, ab eisque exceptus humane petît uti quamprimum ad Alexandrum perduceretur. Cum polliciti essent, tardiores fuerunt idoneum tempus expectantes. Itaque Dinocrates ab his se existimans ludi ab se petît praesidium. Fuerat enim amplissima statura, facie grata, forma dignitateque summa. His igitur naturae muneribus confisus vestimenta posuit in hospitio et oleo corpus perunxit caputque coronavit populea fronde, laevum umerum pelle leonina texit, dextraque clavam tenens incessit contra tribunal regis ius dicentis.
entries.translation: Dinocrates the architect, trusting in his ideas and ingenuity, left Macedonia for the army while Alexander was in power, eager to win the king’s favor. He brought letters from relatives and friends at home to the leading officers and courtiers, hoping to gain easier access. They received him kindly, and he asked to be brought before Alexander as soon as possible. Although they promised to do so, they delayed while waiting for a suitable occasion. Thinking that they were making a fool of him, Dinocrates sought a resource within himself. He was very tall, with a pleasing face and an impressive, dignified physique. Trusting in these natural gifts, he left his clothes at the inn, anointed his body with oil, crowned his head with poplar leaves, draped a lion’s skin over his left shoulder and, holding a club in his right hand, advanced towards the tribunal where the king was administering justice.

entries.latin: Novitas populum cum avertisset, conspexit eum Alexander. Admirans ei iussit locum dari ut accederet, interrogavitque quis esset. At ille: «Dinocrates», inquit, «architectus Macedo, qui ad te cogitationes et formas adfero dignas tuae claritati. Namque Athon montem formavi in statuae virilis figuram, cuius manu laeva designavi civitatis amplissimae moenia, dextera pateram quae exciperet omnium fluminum quae sunt in eo monte aquam, ut inde in mare profunderetur».
entries.translation: The unusual sight drew the crowd’s attention, and Alexander saw him. Astonished, he ordered room to be made for him to approach and asked who he was. “Dinocrates,” he replied, “a Macedonian architect, bringing you ideas and designs worthy of your glory. I have designed Mount Athos in the form of a male statue: in its left hand I have represented the walls of a very large city, and in its right a patera, a ritual bowl, to receive the water of all the mountain’s rivers and pour it into the sea.

entries.latin: Delectatus Alexander ratione formae statim quaesiit, si essent agri circa qui possent frumentaria ratione eam civitatem tueri. Cum invenisset non posse nisi transmarinis subvectionibus, «Dinocrates», inquit, «attendo egregiam formae compositionem et ea delector, sed animadverto si qui deduxerit eo loci coloniam fore ut iudicium eius vituperetur. Ut enim natus infans sine nutricis lacte non potest ali neque ad vitae crescentis gradus perduci, sic civitas sine agris et eorum fructibus in moenibus affluentibus non potest crescere nec sine abundantia cibi frequentiam habere populumque sine copia tueri. Itaque quemadmodum formationem puto probandam, sic iudico locum inprobandum, teque volo esse mecum, quod tua opera sum usurus».
entries.translation: Delighted by the account of the design, Alexander immediately asked whether there was farmland nearby capable of supplying the city with grain. Learning that it could be sustained only by supplies brought from overseas, he said: “Dinocrates, I appreciate the excellence of your design and take pleasure in it, but anyone who founded a colony there would, I see, be criticized for his judgment. Just as a newborn child cannot be nourished without its nurse’s milk or develop through the stages of growing life, so a city cannot grow without farmland and its produce flowing into its walls, maintain a numerous population without abundant food, or sustain its people without supplies. I therefore approve the design but reject the site. Nevertheless, I want you to remain with me, for I shall make use of your services.

entries.latin: Ex eo Dinocrates ab rege non discessit et in Aegyptum est eum persecutus. Ibi Alexander cum animadvertisset portum naturaliter tutum, emporium egregium, campos circa totam Aegyptum frumentarios, inmanis fluminis Nili magnas utilitates, iussit eum suo nomine civitatem Alexandriam constituere. Ita Dinocrates a facie dignitateque corporis commendatus ad eam nobilitatem pervenit. Mihi autem, imperator, staturam non tribuit natura, faciem deformavit aetas, valetudo detraxit vires. Itaque quoniam ab his praesidiis sum desertus, per auxilia scientiae scriptaque ut spero perveniam ad commendationem.
entries.translation: From then on Dinocrates did not leave the king and followed him to Egypt. There, when Alexander had observed a naturally safe harbor, an excellent emporium, corn fields around the whole of Egypt, and the great benefits of the immense river Nile, he ordered him to found the city of Alexandria in his own name. Thus Dinocrates, commended by his face and dignity of body, attained that nobility. But to me, emperor, nature has not given stature, age has disfigured my face, and illness has sapped my strength. Therefore, since I am deserted by these protections, I hope to attain commendation through the aids of science and writings.

entries.latin: Cum autem ⟨quae⟩ primo volumine de officio architecturae terminationibusque artis perscripsi, item de moenibus et intra moenia arearum divisionibus, insequatur ordo de aedibus sacris et publicis aedificiis itemque privatis quibus proportionibus et symmetriis debeant esse uti explicentur, non putavi ante ponendum nisi prius de materiae copiis, e quibus conlatis aedificia structuris et materiationibus perficiuntur, quas habeant in usu virtutes exposuissem quibusque rerum natura e principiis essent temperatae dixissem. Sed antequam naturales res incipiam explicare, de aedificiorum rationibus unde initia ceperint et uti creverint eorum inventiones ante ponam, et insequar ingressus eorum, qui antiquitates rerum naturae et initia humanitatis et inventiones perquisitas scriptorum praeceptis dedicaverunt. Itaque quemadmodum ab his sum institutus exponam.
entries.translation: In the first book I described the architect’s duties and the boundaries of the art, as well as city walls and the division of building plots within them. The next subject in order would be the proportions and commensurabilities required for sacred, public and private buildings. Before that, however, I thought it necessary to explain the properties in use of the materials assembled to complete buildings in masonry and timber, and the natural principles of which those materials are composed. Before discussing their nature, I shall first describe the beginnings of building and the development of its inventions. I shall follow those writers who investigated the early history of nature, the beginnings of human society and its inventions, and committed their precepts to writing. I shall explain these matters as I have learned them from those authors.

entries.latin: Delphicus Apollo Socratem omnium sapientissimum Pythiae responsis est professus. Is autem memoratur prudenter doctissimeque dixisse, oportuisse hominum pectora fenestrata et aperta esse, uti non occultos haberent sensus sed patentes ad considerandum. Utinam vero rerum natura sententiam eius secuta explicata et apparentia ea constituisset! Si enim ita fuisset, non solum laudes aut vitia animorum ad manum aspicerentur, sed etiam disciplinarum scientiae sub oculorum consideratione subiectae non incertis iudiciis probarentur, sed et doctis et scientibus auctoritas egregia et stabilis adderetur ipsique artifices pellicerent sua prudentia, ⟨qui, etiam⟩si non pecunia sint copiosi seu vetustate officinarum habuerint notitiam aut etiam gratia forensi et eloquentia, cum fuerint parati, pro industria studiorum auctoritates possent habere, ut eis, quod profitentur scire, id crederetur. Igitur quoniam haec non ita, sed uti natura rerum voluit, sunt constituta, non efficitur, ut possint homines obscuratis sub pectoribus ingeniis scientias artificiorum penitus latentes, quemadmodum sint, iudicare.
entries.translation: The Delphic Apollo, through the responses of the Pythia, proclaimed Socrates the wisest of all men. Socrates is remembered as having said, with prudence and great learning, that men’s breasts ought to have been fitted with windows and left open, so that their thoughts would not remain hidden but be exposed to examination. Would that nature had followed his judgment and made them manifest and visible! Then not only would the merits or faults of minds be seen at a glance, but the knowledge of the various disciplines, placed before the eyes for examination, would not be exposed to uncertain judgments. The learned and knowledgeable would receive firm and lasting authority, and craftsmen themselves would attract confidence through their understanding: even if they were not wealthy, known through the long standing of their workshops, or furnished with favor in the forum and eloquence, their preparation would win authority commensurate with their diligent studies, so that people would believe that they knew what they professed to know. Since things are constituted otherwise, as nature willed, and men’s talents remain concealed within their breasts, people cannot judge the knowledge peculiar to each art, which lies deeply hidden.

entries.latin: Maxime autem id animadvertere possumus ab antiquis statuariis et pictoribus, quod ex his, qui dignitatis notas et commendationis gratiam habuerunt, aeterna memoria ad posteritatem sunt permanentes, uti Myron, Polycletus, Phidias, Lysippus ceterique, qui nobilitatem ex arte sunt consecuti. Namque ut civitatibus magnis aut regibus aut civibus nobilibus opera fecerunt, ita id sunt adepti. At qui non minore studio et ingenio sollertiaque fuerunt nobilibus et humili fortuna civibus non minus egregie perfecta fecerunt opera, nullam memoriam sunt adsecuti, quod hi non ab industria neque artis sollertia sed a felicitate fuerunt deserti, ut Hegias Atheniensis, Chion Corinthius, Myagrus Phocaeus, Pharax Ephesius, Boedas Byzantius etiamque alii plures. Non minus item pictores, uti Aristomenes Thasius, Polycles et Androcydes ⟨Cyzice⟩ni, Theo Magnes ceterique, quos neque industria neque artis studium neque sollertia defecit, sed aut rei familiaris exiguitas aut inbecillitas fortunae seu in ambitione certationis contrariorum superatio obstitit eorum dignitati.
entries.translation: This can be seen above all in the sculptors and painters of old. Those who enjoyed marks of distinction and the favor of recommendation remain in everlasting memory among posterity—Myron, Polyclitus, Phidias, Lysippus and the others who won renown through their art. They achieved it because they made works for great cities, kings or noble citizens. Others, with no less zeal, talent and skill, made works no less admirably finished for citizens both noble and of modest means, yet obtained no remembrance: they were forsaken not by diligence or artistic skill, but by good fortune. Such were Hegias of Athens, Chion of Corinth, Myagrus of Phocaea, Pharax of Ephesus, Boedas of Byzantium and many more. Likewise among painters there were Aristomenes of Thasos, Polycles and Androcydes of Cyzicus, Theon of Magnesia and the others, who lacked neither diligence, artistic commitment nor skill, but whose standing was obstructed by a small patrimony, adverse fortune or the superiority of rivals in the competition for distinction.

entries.latin: Nec tamen est admirandum, si propter ignotitiam artis virtutes obscurantur, sed maxime indignandum, cum etiam saepe eblandiatur gratia conviviorum a veris iudiciis falsam probationem. Ergo, uti Socrati placuit, si ita sensus et sententiae scientiaeque disciplinis auctae perspicuae et perlucidae fuissent, non gratia neque ambitio valeret, sed si qui veris certisque laboribus doctrinarum pervenissent ad scientiam summam, eis ultro opera traderentur. Quoniam autem ea non sunt inlustria neque apparentia in aspectu, ut putamus oportuisse, et animadverto potius indoctos quam doctos gratia superare, non esse certandum iudicans cum indoctis ambitione, potius his praeceptis editis ostendam nostrae scientiae virtutem.
entries.translation: It is no wonder that merit is obscured through ignorance of the art; but it is especially a cause for indignation when favor won at banquets often coaxes a false approval from true judgment. As Socrates wished, had perceptions, opinions and knowledge enriched by the disciplines been clear and transparent, neither favor nor ambition would prevail: works would be entrusted spontaneously to those who had attained the highest knowledge through genuine and sound scholarly labor. Since these things are neither manifest nor visible, as we think they ought to be, and I observe that the unlearned more often surpass the learned through favor, I judge that I should not compete with the unlearned in ambition. I shall instead show the worth of our knowledge by publishing these precepts.

entries.latin: Itaque, imperator, in primo volumine tibi de arte et quas habeat ea virtutes quibusque disciplinis oporteat esse auctum architectum exposui, et subieci causas quid ita earum oporteat eum esse peritum, rationesque summae architecturae partitione distribui finitionibusque terminavi. deinde quod erat primum et necessarium, de moenibus quemadmodum eligantur loci salubres ratiocinationibus explicui, ventique qui sint et e quibus <regionibus> singuli spirant deformationibus grammicis ostendi, platearumque et vicorum uti emendate fiant distributiones in moenibus docui et ita finitionem primo volumine constitui. item in secundo de materia quas habeat in operibus utilitates et quibus virtutibus e natura rerum est comparata peregi. nunc in tertio de deorum inmortalium aedibus sacris dicam et uti oportet perscriptas exponam.
entries.translation: Accordingly, Emperor, in the first book I set forth for you what the art is, what virtues it possesses, and in what disciplines the architect ought to be trained; I added the reasons why he must be skilled in them, distributed the whole of architecture by a division, and defined it by definitions. Then, treating what was first and most necessary, I explained by reasoned argument how, in laying out city walls, to choose healthy sites; I showed by linear diagrams which the winds are and from what regions each blows; I taught how the streets and lanes within the walls may be correctly laid out, and so brought the first book to a close. In the second I dealt with materials—what advantages they afford in works, and with what qualities Nature has endowed them. Now, in the third, I shall speak of the sacred temples of the immortal gods and set them forth, as is fitting, in full detail.

entries.latin: Cum animadvertissem, imperator, plures de architectura praecepta voluminaque commentariorum non ordinata sed incepta uti particulas errabundas reliquisse, dignam et utilissimam rem putavi tantae disciplinae corpus ad perfectam ordinationem perducere et praescriptas in singulis voluminibus singulorum generum qualitates explicare. itaque, Caesar, primo volumine tibi de officio eius et quibus eruditum esse rebus architectum oporteat exposui. secundo de copiis materiae, e quibus aedificia constituuntur, disputavi. tertio autem de aedium sacrarum dispositionibus et de earum generum varietate quasque et quot habeant species earumque quae sunt in singulis generibus distributiones,
entries.translation: Having observed, Emperor, that many had left the precepts and volumes of commentaries on architecture not set in order but merely begun, like scattered fragments, I judged it a worthy and most useful thing to bring the body of so great a discipline to a perfect ordering, and to set forth, in each volume, the prescribed qualities of each of the kinds. And so, Caesar, in the first book I expounded to you the office of the architect and in what subjects he ought to be trained; in the second I treated of the materials from which buildings are constructed; and in the third, of the arrangement of sacred temples, of the variety of their kinds, how many and what species they have, and what in each kind are their distributions.

entries.latin: ex tribus generibus, quae subtilissimas haberent proportionibus modulorum quantitates, ionici generis moribus docui. nunc hoc volumine de doricis corinthiisque constitutis et omnibus dicam eorumque discrimina et proprietates explicabo.
entries.translation: Of the three orders that possess the most subtle proportions in the quantity of their modules, I set forth the usages of the Ionic; now, in this volume, I shall speak of the established principles of the Doric and the Corinthian, and explain their differences and properties.

entries.latin: Qui amplioribus voluminibus, imperator, ingenii cogitationes praeceptaque explicaverunt, maximas et egregias adiecerunt suis scriptis auctoritates. quod etiam velim nostris quoque studiis res pateretur, ut amplificationibus auctoritas et in his praeceptis augeretur, sed id non est quemadmodum putatur expeditum. non enim de architectura sic scribitur uti historia aut poemata. historiae per se tenent lectores. habent enim novarum rerum varias expectationes. poematorum vero [carminum] metra et pedes ac verborum elegans dispositio et sententiarum inter personas distinctas [versuum] pronuntiatio prolectando sensus legentium perducit sine offensa ad summam scriptorum terminationem.
entries.translation: Those who have expounded their ideas and precepts in more extensive volumes, Emperor, have lent their writings considerable distinction and authority. I too should wish the subject of our studies to permit such expansiveness, so that greater length might enhance the authority of these teachings; but this is less straightforward than one might suppose. Architecture cannot be written about in the same way as history or poetry. History holds the reader’s attention through the prospect of varied new events; poetry, through its meters, rhythms, elegant arrangement of words and speeches assigned to different characters, carries the reader’s attention smoothly to the conclusion of the work.

entries.latin: id autem in architecturae conscriptionibus non potest fieri, quod vocabula ex artis propria necessitate concepta inconsueto sermone obiciunt sensibus obscuritatem. cum ergo ea per se non sint aperta nec pateant eorum in consuetudine nomina, tum etiam praeceptorum late vagantes scripturae, si non contrahentur, ut paucis et perlucidis sententiis explicentur, frequentia multitudineque sermonis inpediente incertas legentium efficient cogitationes. itaque occultas nominationes commensusque e membris operum pronuntians, ut memoriae tradantur, breviter exponam. sic enim expeditius ea recipere poterunt mentes.
entries.translation: Architectural writing cannot achieve the same effect, because the technical vocabulary required by the art is unfamiliar and difficult for readers. If the exposition also wanders at length instead of being compressed into a few clear statements, the quantity of words will confuse their understanding. I shall therefore explain unfamiliar terms and the measured relationships of architectural members briefly, so that they can be remembered and more readily understood.

entries.latin: non minus cum animadvertissem distentam occupationibus civitatem publicis et privatis negotiis, paucis iudicavi scribendum, uti angusto spatio vacuitatis ea legentes breviter percipere possent. Etiamque Pythagorae quique eius haeresim fuerunt secuti placuit cybicis rationibus praecepta in voluminibus scribere, constitueruntque cybum CCXVI versus eosque non plus tres in una conscriptione oportere esse putaverunt.
entries.translation: Seeing also that the citizens were occupied with public and private affairs, I judged that I should write briefly, so that they could grasp my subject during their limited leisure. Pythagoras and the followers of his school likewise chose to set down their precepts in books on a cubic principle: they made one cube consist of 216 verses and thought that no more than three such units should appear in a single composition.

entries.latin: Cybus autem est corpus ex lateribus aequali latitudine planitiarum perquadratum. is cum est iactus, quam in partem incubuit dum est intactus inmotam habet stabilitatem, uti sunt etiam tesserae quas in alveo ludentes iaciunt. hanc autem similitudinem ex eo sumpsisse videntur quod is numerus versuum uti cybus in quemcumque sensum insederit, inmotam efficiat ibi memoriae stabilitatem. Graeci quoque poetae comici interponentes e choro canticum diviserunt spatia fabularum. ita partes cybica ratione facientes intercapedinibus levant actorum pronuntiationes.
entries.translation: A cube is a solid bounded by equal square faces. When thrown, it remains stable on whichever face it rests, provided it is left untouched, like the dice cast by players into a gaming tray. The comparison seems to have been adopted because this number of verses, once established in the mind as a cube rests on a face, would give memory a similar stability. Greek comic poets also divided their plays by inserting songs for the chorus. By organizing the parts on a cubic principle, they relieved the actors’ delivery with intervals.

entries.latin: Cum ergo haec naturali modo sint a maioribus observata animoque advertam inusitatas et obscuras multis res esse mihi scribendas, quo facilius ad sensus legentium pervenire possint, brevibus voluminibus iudicavi scribere. ita enim expedita erunt ad intellegendum. eorumque ordinationes institui uti non sint quaerentibus separatim colligenda, sed e corpore uno et in singulis voluminibus generum haberent explicationes. itaque, Caesar, tertio et quarto volumine aedium sacrarum rationes exposui, hoc libro publicorum locorum expediam dispositiones. primumque forum uti oporteat constitui dicam, quod in eo et publicarum et privatarum rerum rationes per magistratus gubernantur.
entries.translation: Since our predecessors observed these principles in a natural way, and since I must discuss matters unfamiliar and obscure to many readers, I have chosen to write short books that make them easier to understand. I have arranged the material so that readers need not gather it from separate sources: the work forms a single body, with each book explaining a particular class of subjects. Thus, Caesar, after setting out the principles of sacred buildings in the third and fourth books, I shall explain the arrangement of public places in this one. I shall begin with the forum, where magistrates administer public and private affairs.

entries.latin: Aristippus philosophus Socraticus naufragio cum eiectus ad Rhodiensium litus animadvertisset geometrica schemata descripta, exclamavisse ad comites ita dicitur bene speremus, hominum enim vestigia video statimque in oppidum Rhodum contendit et recta gymnasium devenit, ibique de philosophia disputans muneribus est donatus, ut non tantum se ornaret sed etiam eis qui una fuerunt et vestitum et cetera quae opus essent ad victum praestaret. cum autem eius comites in patriam reverti voluissent interrogarentque eum quidnam vellet domum renuntiari, tunc ita mandavit dicere, eiusmodi possessiones et viatica liberis oportere parari quae etiam e naufragio una possent enatare.
entries.translation: Aristippus, the Socratic philosopher, shipwrecked and cast ashore on the coast of Rhodes, noticed geometrical figures drawn in the sand and is said to have cried out to his companions: “Let us be of good hope, for I see the traces of men.” He made at once for the city of Rhodes and went straight to the gymnasium, where, discoursing on philosophy, he was rewarded with gifts so generous that he could provide not only for himself but also for those who were with him, with clothing and everything else needed for life. When his companions wished to return home and asked what message he would have them carry back, he bade them say this: that children ought to be furnished with such possessions and such provisions for the journey as could swim ashore with them even from a shipwreck.

entries.latin: namque ea vera praesidia sunt vitae quibus neque fortunae tempestas iniqua neque publicarum rerum mutatio neque belli vastatio potest nocere. non minus eam sententiam augendo Theophrastus, hortando doctos potius esse quam pecuniae confidentes ita ponit, doctum ex omnibus solum neque in alienis locis peregrinum neque amissis familiaribus et necessariis inopem amicorum sed in omni civitate esse civem difficilesque fortunae sine timore posse despicere casus, at qui non doctrinarum sed felicitatis praesidiis putaret se esse vallatum, labidis itineribus vadentem non stabili sed infirma conflictari vita.
entries.translation: For these are the true safeguards of life: neither the adverse storms of fortune, nor upheavals in public affairs, nor the devastation of war can harm them. Theophrastus develops the same idea, urging people to become learned rather than to put their trust in wealth. The educated person alone is not a stranger in foreign lands or left without friends when family and companions are lost; in every city such a person is a citizen and can face the hazards of fortune without fear. By contrast, one who trusts in good luck rather than learning walks on slippery paths and struggles through a fragile, uncertain life.

entries.latin: Epicurus vero non dissimiliter ait pauca sapientibus fortunam tribuere, quae autem maxima et necessaria sunt, animi mentisque cogitationibus gubernari. haec ita etiam plures philosophi dixerunt. non minus poetae qui antiquas comoedias graece scripserunt, easdem sententias versibus in scaena pronuntiaverunt, ut Crates Chionides Aristophanes, maxime etiam cum his Alexis, qui Athenienses ait oportere ideo laudari quod omnium Graecorum leges cogunt parentes <ali> a liberis, Atheniensium non omnes nisi eos qui liberos artibus erudissent. omnia enim munera fortunae cum dantur ab ea faciliter adimuntur, disciplinae vero coniunctae cum animis nullo tempore deficiunt, sed permanent stabiliter ad summum exitum vitae.
entries.translation: Epicurus likewise says that fortune grants the wise relatively little, whereas the greatest and most necessary matters are governed by thought and judgment. Many other philosophers held the same view. The authors of ancient Greek comedy — Crates, Chionides, Aristophanes and, above all, Alexis — expressed similar ideas on stage. Alexis praises the Athenians because, whereas Greek laws generally require children to support their parents, the Athenians impose that duty only in respect of parents who have taught their children an art. Fortune may take away everything it has given; learning, once joined to the mind, remains steadfast to the end of life.

entries.latin: itaque ego maximas infinitasque parentibus ago atque habeo gratias, quod Atheniensium legem probantes me arte erudiendum curaverunt, et ea quae non potest esse probata sine litteratura encyclioque doctrinarum omnium disciplina. cum ergo et parentium cura et praeceptorum doctrinis auctas haberem copias disciplinarum, philologis et philotechnis rebus commentariorumque scripturis me delectans eas possessiones animo paravi, e quibus haec est fructuum summa, nullas plus habendi esse necessitates eamque esse proprietatem divitiarum maxime, nihil desiderare. sed forte nonnulli haec levia iudicantes putant eos esse sapientes qui pecunia sunt copiosi. itaque plerique ad id propositum contendentes audacia adhibita cum divitiis etiam notitiam sunt consecuti.
entries.translation: I therefore give and owe the greatest, indeed boundless, thanks to my parents, who, approving the law of the Athenians, took care that I should be trained in an art, and in one that cannot be mastered without letters and the encyclopedic education that embraces all the disciplines. Having thus enlarged my store of learning through my parents’ care and my teachers’ instruction, and delighting in literary and technical studies and in the writing of treatises, I acquired for my mind possessions whose chief fruit is this: that one has no need to possess more, and that the truest property of wealth is to desire nothing. Some, perhaps, think these things of little account and hold that the wise are those who abound in money. Many, therefore, pursuing that aim with boldness, have won notoriety together with riches.

entries.latin: ego autem, Caesar, non ad pecuniam parandam ex arte dedi studium, sed potius tenuitatem cum bona fama quam abundantiam cum infamia sequendam probavi. ideo notities parum est adsecuta. sed tamen his voluminibus editis, ut spero, etiam posteris ero notus. neque est mirandum quid ita pluribus sim ignotus. ceteri architecti rogant et ambiunt ut architectent, mihi autem a praeceptoribus est traditum rogatum non rogantem oportere suscipere curam, quod ingenuus color movetur pudore petendo rem suspiciosam. nam beneficium dantes non accipientes ambiuntur. quid enim putemus suspicari qui rogetur de patrimonio sumptus faciendos committere gratiae petentis, nisi praedae compendiique eius causa iudicet faciundum?.
entries.translation: I, however, Caesar, have not applied myself to making money by my art; I have preferred slender means with a good name to abundance with disrepute. For this reason I have gained little renown. Yet, now that these volumes are published, I hope to be known even to posterity. Nor should it surprise anyone that I am unknown to so many. Other architects solicit and canvass for commissions; but I was taught by my masters that one should undertake a charge when asked, not by asking, because a freeborn man’s complexion is changed by shame when he petitions for something that arouses suspicion. For it is those who confer a favor who are courted, not those who receive it. What, then, are we to suppose a man suspects when he is asked to entrust the spending of his patrimony to the goodwill of a petitioner, if not that the petitioner judges the work worth doing for his own plunder and profit?

entries.latin: itaque maiores primum a genere probatis operam tradebant architectis, deinde quaerebant si honeste essent educati, ingenuo pudori non audaciae protervitatis permittendum iudicantes. ipsi autem artifices non erudiebant nisi suos liberos aut cognatos et eos viros bonos instituebant, quibus tantarum rerum fidei pecuniae sine dubitatione permitterentur. Cum autem animadverto ab indoctis et inperitis tantae disciplinae magnitudinem iactari et ab îs qui non modo <> architecturae sed omnino ne fabricae quidem notitiam habent, non possum non laudare patres familiarum eos qui litteraturae fiducia confirmati per se aedificantes ita iudicant, si inperitis sit committendum, ipsos potius digniores esse ad suam voluntatem quam ad alienam pecuniae consumere summam.
entries.translation: Our predecessors therefore entrusted building works first to architects whose family standing had been tested, and then enquired whether they had received an honorable education. They judged that responsibility should rest with the restraint of a freeborn man, rather than the audacity of the shameless. Craftsmen themselves trained only their sons or relatives, forming them as upright men to whose integrity funds for important works could safely be entrusted. Yet when I see so great a discipline handled at the whim of the uneducated and inexperienced, including men who know neither architecture nor even the craft of building, I cannot but commend those householders who, trusting in their literary education, build for themselves. If the work must be entrusted to the inexperienced, they judge themselves more entitled to spend their money according to their own judgment than according to someone else’s.

entries.latin: itaque nemo artem ullam aliam conatur domi facere, uti sutrinam fullonicam aut ex ceteris quae sunt faciliores, nisi architecturam, ideo quod qui profitentur non arte vera sed falso nominantur architecti. quas ob res corpus architecturae rationesque eius putavi diligentissime conscribendas, opinans munus omnibus gentibus non ingratum futurum. igitur quoniam in quinto de opportunitate communium operum perscripsi, in hoc volumine privatorum aedificiorum ratiocinationes et commensus symmetriarum explicabo.
entries.translation: Thus no one attempts to practise any other art at home — shoemaking, fulling or any of the other easier crafts — except architecture, because those who profess it are called architects not by virtue of true art but falsely. For these reasons I judged that the body of architecture and its principles should be set down with the utmost care, believing that this would be a service not unwelcome to all peoples. Accordingly, since in the fifth book I have written of the fitness of public works, in this volume I shall set out the principles of private buildings and the commensurability of their proportions.

entries.latin: Maiores cum sapienter tum etiam utiliter instituerunt, per commentariorum relationes cogitata tradere posteris, ut ea non interirent sed singulis aetatibus crescentia voluminibus edita gradatim pervenirent vetustatibus ad summam doctrinarum subtilitatem. itaque non mediocres sed infinitae sunt his agendae gratiae, quod non invidiose silentes praetermiserunt, sed omnium generum sensus conscriptionibus memoriae tradendos curaverunt.
entries.translation: The ancients, both wisely and usefully, instituted the transmission of their thoughts to posterity through the reports of their commentaries, so that they would not perish, but, published in increasing volumes in each age, would gradually reach the highest subtlety of their doctrines. Therefore, the merits of this work are not moderate but infinite, because they did not pass over it in envious silence, but took care to transmit to memory all kinds of thoughts in writings.

entries.latin: namque si non ita fecissent, non potuissemus scire quae res in Troia fuissent gestae, nec quid Thales Democritus Anaxagoras Xenophanes reliquique physici sensissent de rerum natura quasque Socrates Platon Aristoteles Zenon Epicurus aliique philosophi hominibus agendae vitae terminationes finissent seu Croesus Alexander Darius ceterique reges quas res aut quibus rationibus gessissent fuissent notae, nisi maiores praeceptorum comparationibus omnium memoriae ad posteritatem commentariis extulissent.
entries.translation: For if they had not done so, we would not have been able to know what things had been done in Troy, nor what Thales, Democritus, Anaxagoras, Xenophanes, and the other natural philosophers had thought about the nature of things, nor what Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Zeno, Epicurus, and other philosophers had concluded the ends of life for men, nor what things Croesus, Alexander, Darius, and the other kings had done, or for what reasons, would have been known, unless the elders had brought forth the memory of all things in their commentaries by comparisons of precepts for posterity.

entries.latin: itaque quemadmodum his gratiae sunt agendae, contra qui eorum scripta furantes pro suis praedicant sunt vituperandi, quique non propriis cogitationibus scriptorum nituntur, sed invidis moribus aliena violantes gloriantur, non modo sunt reprehendendi, sed etiam quia impio more vixerunt, poena condemnandi. nec tamen haec res non vindicatae curiosius ab antiquis esse memorantur. quorum exitus iudiciorum qui fuerint, non est alienum quemadmodum sint nobis traditi explicare.
entries.translation: Just as gratitude is owed to those who transmit their thoughts, so those who steal others’ writings and proclaim them their own deserve condemnation. Those who claim glory by violating the work of others, instead of relying on their own ideas, merit not merely reproach but punishment for acting dishonourably. Such offenses, it is reported, did not go unpunished among the ancients. It is therefore appropriate to recount the outcomes of those judgments as they have been handed down to us.

entries.latin: reges Attalici magnis philologiae dulcedinibus inducti cum egregiam bybliothecam Pergami ad communem delectationem instituissent, tunc item Ptolomaeus infinito zelo cupiditatisque incitatus studio non minoribus industriis ad eundem modum contenderat Alexandriae comparare. cum autem summa diligentia perfecisset, non putavit id satis esse nisi propagationibus inseminando curaret augendam. itaque Musis et Apollini ludos dedicavit et quemadmodum athletarum sic communium scriptorum victoribus praemia et honores constituit.
entries.translation: When the Attalic kings, led by the great delights of philology, had established an excellent library at Pergamum for the common enjoyment, then likewise Ptolemy, inspired by infinite zeal and desire, strove with no less diligence to furnish Alexandria with the same. But when he had accomplished it with the utmost diligence, he did not think that it was sufficient unless he took care to increase it by insemination. Accordingly he dedicated games to the Muses and Apollo, and, as he did to athletes, so he established prizes and honors for the victors of common writings.

entries.latin: his ita institutis cum ludi adessent, iudices litterati qui ea probarent erant legendi. rex cum iam sex civitatis lectos habuisset nec tam cito septumum idoneum inveniret, retulit ad eos qui supra bybliothecam fuerunt et quaesiit si quem novissent ad id expeditum. tunc ei dixerunt esse quendam Aristophanen, qui summo studio summaque diligentia cotidie omnes libros ex ordine perlegeret. itaque conventu ludorum cum secretae sedes iudicibus essent distributae, cum ceteris Aristophanes citatus quemadmodum fuerat locus ei designatus sedit.
entries.translation: As the games approached, learned judges had to be selected to assess them. The king had already chosen six men from the city but could not readily find a suitable seventh. He consulted those in charge of the library and asked whether they knew anyone qualified. They told him of a certain Aristophanes, who read through all the books in order each day with exceptional diligence and attention. When the games assembled and reserved seats had been assigned to the judges, Aristophanes was summoned with the others and took his appointed place.

entries.latin: primo poetarum ordine ad certationem inducto cum recitarentur scripta, populus cunctus significando monebat iudices quod probarent. itaque cum ab singulis sententiae sunt rogatae, sex una dixerunt et quem maxime animadverterunt multitudini placuisse, ei primum praemium, insequenti secundum tribuerunt. Aristophanes vero cum ab eo sententia rogaretur, eum primum renuntiari iussit qui minime populo placuisset.
entries.translation: When the first order of poets was brought to the competition, and their writings were recited, the whole people indicated by signs to the judges what they should approve. Accordingly, when each was asked for his opinion, the six gave one, and to him whom they observed had most pleased the multitude, they awarded the first prize, and to the next the second. But Aristophanes, when his opinion was asked of him, ordered that the one who had least pleased the people be dismissed first.

entries.latin: cum autem rex et universi vehementer indignarentur, surrexit et rogando impetravit ut paterentur se dicere. itaque silentio facto docuit unum ex his eum esse poetam, ceteros aliena recitavisse, oportere autem iudicantes non furta sed scripta probare. admirante populo et rege dubitante, fretus memoriae certis armariis infinita volumina eduxit et ea cum recitatis conferendo coegit ipsos furatos de se confiteri. itaque rex iussit cum his agi furti condemnatosque cum ignominia dimisit, Aristophanen vero amplissimis muneribus ornavit et supra bybliothecam constituit.
entries.translation: But when the king and all were greatly indignant, he rose and begged that they be allowed to speak. So, by making silence, he taught that one of them was a poet, and that the others had recited other people's works, but that they judged it necessary to prove that they were not stolen but written. With the people astonished and the king doubtful, he, relying on his memory, brought out an infinite number of volumes from certain cupboards and, comparing them with the ones recited, forced the thieves themselves to confess that they had stolen them. So the king ordered that these be tried and those convicted of theft were released with disgrace, but Aristophanes was adorned with the most magnificent gifts and placed over the library.

entries.latin: insequentibus annis a Macedonia Zoilus, qui adoptavit cognomen ut Homeromastix vocitaretur, Alexandriam venit suaque scripta contra Iliadem et Odyssean comparata regi recitavit. Ptolomaeus vero cum animadvertisset poetarum parentem philologiaeque omnis ducem absentem vexari et cuius ab cunctis gentibus scripta suspicerentur ab eo vituperari, indignans nullum ei dedit responsum. Zoilus autem cum diutius in regno fuisset, inopia pressus summisit ad regem postulans ut aliquid sibi tribueretur.
entries.translation: In the following years, Zoilus, who adopted the surname Homeromastix, came from Macedonia to Alexandria and read his writings against the Iliad and the Odyssey to the king, having prepared them. But Ptolemy, when he perceived that the father of poets and the leader of all philology was being harassed in his absence, and that his writings, whose writings were highly regarded by all nations, were being censured by him, became indignant and gave him no answer. But Zoilus, when he had been in the kingdom for a long time, was pressed by poverty and sent to the king, requesting that something be given to him.

entries.latin: rex vero respondisse dicitur Homerum, qui ante annos mille decessisset, aevo perpetuo multa milia hominum pascere, item debere qui meliore ingenio se profiteretur non modo unum sed etiam plures alere posse. et ad summam mors eius ut parricidii damnati varie memoratur. alii enim scripserunt a Philadelpho esse in crucem fixum, nonnulli Chii lapides esse coniectos, alii Zmyrnae vivum in pyram coniectum. quorum utrum ei acciderit, merenti digna constitit poena. non enim aliter videtur promereri qui citat eos quorum responsum, quid senserint scribentes, non potest coram indicari.
entries.translation: The king is said to have replied that Homer, who died a thousand years ago, would feed many thousands of men in perpetuity, and that he who would claim to be superior in genius should be able to feed not only one but also many. And to sum up, his death as a condemned parricide is variously recorded. For some have written that he was crucified at Philadelphia, some that he was stoned at Chios, others that he was thrown alive on a pyre at Smyrna. Whether any of these things happened to him, the punishment he deserved was decidedly worthy. For it does not seem that he deserves otherwise who quotes those whose response, what they thought when writing, cannot be stated in person.

entries.latin: ego vero, Caesar, neque alienis indicibus mutatis interposito nomine meo id profero corpus neque ullius cogitata vituperans institui ex eo me adprobare, sed omnibus scriptoribus infinitas ago gratias quod egregiis ingeniorum sollertiis ex aevo conlatis abundantes alius alio genere copias praeparaverunt, unde nos uti fontibus haurientes aquam et ad propria proposita traducentes facundiores et expeditiores habemus ad scribendum facultates talibusque confidentes auctoribus audemus institutiones novas comparare.
entries.translation: But I, Caesar, neither do I produce this body with my own name interposed, having altered the evidence of others, nor do I set out to approve myself by criticizing the thoughts of anyone, but I give infinite thanks to all writers, who, with the excellent skills of their geniuses, brought together from time immemorial, have prepared abundant resources of one kind or another, from which we, drawing water as from springs and translating it for our own purposes, have more eloquent and expeditious faculties for writing, and, trusting in such authors, we dare to compare new compositions.

entries.latin: Igitur tales ingressus eorum quia ad propositi mei rationes animadverti praeparatos, inde sumendo progredi coepi. namque primum Agatharchus Athenis Aeschylo docente tragoediam scaenam fecit et de ea commentarium reliquit. ex eo moniti Democritus et Anaxagoras de eadem re scripserunt, quemadmodum oporteat ad aciem oculorum radiorumque extentionem certo loco centro constituto lineas ratione naturali respondere, uti de certa re certae imagines aedificiorum in scaenarum picturis redderent speciem et quae in directis planisque frontibus sint figurata, alia abscedentia, alia prominentia esse videantur.
entries.translation: Therefore, such were their entrances, because I observed that the reasons for my purpose were prepared, and I proceeded from there with strength. For first Agatharchus, under the instruction of Aeschylus, staged a tragedy in Athens and left a commentary on it. From him, Democritus and Anaxagoras, advised, wrote on the same subject, how it is necessary for lines to correspond by natural reason to the line of sight and the extension of rays, with a center established at a certain place, so that from an uncertain thing certain images of buildings in stage paintings might give the appearance, and those which are figured on straight and flat fronts might seem to be otherwise absurdly prominent.

entries.latin: postea Silenus de symmetriis doricorum edidit volumen, de aede Iunonis quae est Sami dorica Theodorus, ionice Ephesi quae est Dianae Chersiphron et Metagenes, de fano Minervae quod est Priene ionicum Pytheos, item de aede Minervae dorice quae est Athenis in arce Ictinos et Carpion, Theodorus Phocaeus de tholo qui est Delphis, Philo de aedium sacrarum symmetriis et de armamentario quod fuerat Piraei portu, Hermogenes de aede Dianae ionice quae est Magnesia pseudodipteros et Liberi Patris Teo monopteros, item Arcesius de symmetriis corinthiis et ionico Trallibus Aesculapio quod etiam ipse sua manu dicitur fecisse, de Mausoleo Satyrus et Pytheos, quibus vero felicitas maximum summumque contulit munus.
entries.translation: Later Silenus published a volume on the symmetries of the Dorics, Theodorus on the temple of Juno, which is the Doric temple of Samos, and Metagenes on the Ionic temple of Ephesus, which is the temple of Diana, Chersiphron and Metagenes, on the temple of Minerva, which is the Ionic temple of Priene, Pytheos, likewise on the Doric temple of Minerva, which is in Athens in the citadel of Ictions and Carpion, Theodore Phocaeus on the tholos which is at Delphi, Philo on the symmetries of sacred buildings and on the armoury which he had made in the port of Piraeus, Hermogenes on the Ionic temple of Diana, which is the temple of Magnesia, and the Theomonopteros of Liberi Patris, Arcesius on the symmetries of Corinth and the Ionic temple of Aesculapius at Trallis, which he himself is said to have made with his own hand, and Satyrs and Pytheos on the Mausoleum, to which, however, fortune bestowed the greatest and most sublime gift.

entries.latin: quorum enim artes aevo perpetuo nobilissimas laudes et sempiterno florentes habere iudicantur, ei cogitatis egregias operas praestiterunt. namque singulis frontibus singuli artifices sumpserunt certatim partes ad ornandum et probandum Leochares Bryaxis Scopas Praxiteles, nonnulli etiam putant Timotheum, quorum artis eminens excellentia coegit ad septem spectaculorum eius operis pervenire famam.
entries.translation: For their arts are judged to have the most noble praises throughout the ages and to flourish for ever, and they have produced excellent works of design. For on each front, individual artists competed to adorn and prove Leochares, Bryaxis, Scopas, Praxiteles, and some even think Timotheus, whose eminent excellence of art forced the fame of his work to reach seven spectacles.

entries.latin: praeterea minus nobiles multi praecepta symmetriarum conscripserunt, uti Nexaris Theocydes Demophilos Pollis Leonidas Silanion Melampus Sarnacus Euphranor. non minus de machinationibus, uti Diades Archytas Archimedes Ctesibios Nymphodorus Philo Byzantius Diphilos Democles Charias Polyidos Pyrros Agesistratos. quorum ex commentariis quae utilia esse his rebus animadverti, collecta in unum coegi corpus, et ideo maxime, quod animadverti in ea re ab Graecis volumina plura edita, ab nostris oppido quam pauca. Fuficius enim nimirum de his rebus primus instituit edere volumen, item Terentius Varro de novem disciplinis unum de architectura, P. Septimius duo.
entries.translation: Moreover, many less noble men wrote precepts on symmetry, such as Theocides of Nexaris, Demophilus, Pollis, Leonidas, Silanion, Melampus, Sarnacus, Euphranor. No less on engineering, such as Diades, Archytas, Archimedes, Ctesibius, Nymphodorus, Philo, Byzantius, Diphilus, Democles, Charias, Polyides, Pyrrhus, Agesistratus. From whose commentaries I have observed to be useful in these matters, I have collected several volumes on this subject published by the Greeks, and more than a few by our own people. Fuficius was the first to undertake to publish a volume on these matters, as was Terentius Varro, one on the nine disciplines, on architecture, and Publius Septimius, two.

entries.latin: amplius vero in id genus scripturae adhuc nemo incubuisse videtur, cum fuissent et antiqui cives magni architecti, qui potuissent non minus eleganter scripta comparare. namque Athenis Antistates et Callaeschros et Antimachides et Porinos architecti Pisistrato aedem Iovi Olympio facienti fundamenta constituerunt, post mortem autem eius propter interpellationem reipublicae incepta reliquerunt. itaque circiter annis <quadringentis> post Antiochus rex cum in id opus inpensam esset pollicitus, cellae magnitudinem et columnarum circa dipteron conlocationem epistyliorumque et ceterorum ornamentorum ad symmetriam distributionem magna sollertia scientiaque summa civis Romanus Cossutius nobiliter est architectatus. id autem opus non modo vulgo sed etiam in paucis a magnificentia nominatur.
entries.translation: But no one seems to have yet devoted himself more to that kind of writing, since there were also great architects among the ancient citizens who could have produced writings no less elegantly. For at Athens the architects Antistates and Callaeschros and Antimachides and Phormus laid the foundations of the temple of Jupiter Olympias which Pisistratus was building, but after his death they abandoned the projects because of the interruption of the state. Accordingly, about four hundred years later, when King Antiochus had promised to spend on that work, the size of the room and the arrangement of the columns around the dipteron and the distribution of the epistyles and other ornaments in a symmetrical manner were nobly designed by the Roman citizen Cossutius with great skill and supreme knowledge. And that work is not only popularly but also in a few places by its magnificence.

entries.latin: nam quattuor locis sunt aedium sacrarum marmoreis operibus ornatae dispositiones, e quibus propriae de his nominationes clarissima fama nominantur. quorum excellentiae prudentesque cogitationum apparatus suspectus habent in deorum σημαντικοῖς. primumque aedes Ephesi Dianae ionico genere ab Chersiphrone Gnosio et filio eius Metagene est instituta, quam postea Demetrius ipsius Dianae servus et Paeonius Ephesius dicuntur perfecisse. Mileti Apollini item ionicis symmetriis ⟨aedem⟩ idem Paeonius Daphnisque Milesius instituerunt. Eleusine Cereris et Proserpinae cellam inmani magnitudine Ictinos dorico more sine exterioribus columnis ad laxamentum usus sacrificiorum pertexit.
entries.translation: For in four places there are arrangements of sacred buildings adorned with marble works, from which the most famous names are properly named. The excellences and prudent arrangements of which are suspected in the ceremony of the gods. The first temple of Diana at Ephesus was erected in the Ionic style by Chersiphron of Gnosius and his son Metagenes, which is said to have been completed afterwards by Demetrius, the servant of Diana herself, and Paeonius of Ephesus. The same was erected in the Ionic style by Paeonius and Daphnis of Miles. The cella of Ceres and Proserpina at Eleusis was built in the Doric style without exterior columns for the relaxation of sacrifices.

entries.latin: eam autem postea cum Demetrius Phalereus Athenis rerum potiretur, Philo ante templum in fronte columnis constitutis prostylon fecit. ita aucto vestibulo laxamentum initiantibus operique summam adiecit auctoritatem. in asty vero Olympium amplo modulorum comparatu corinthiis symmetriis et proportionibus, uti supra scriptum est, architectandum Cossutius suscepisse memoratur, cuius commentarium nullum est inventum. nec tamen a Cossutio solum de his rebus scripta sunt desideranda sed etiam a G. Mucio, qui magna scientia confisus aedis Honoris et Virtutis Marianae cellae columnarumque et epistyliorum symmetrias legitimis artis institutis perfecit. id vero si marmoreum fuisset, ut haberet quemadmodum ab arte subtilitatem sic ab magnificentia et inpensis auctoritatem, in primis et summis operibus nominaretur.
entries.translation: But later, when Demetrius Phalerum took possession of Athens, Philo built a prostylon in front of the temple with columns set in front. Having thus built the vestibule, he added a great deal of authority to the workmen who were beginning it. But in Asty, when the Olympos were compared in ample dimensions with the Corinthian symmetries and proportions, as has been written above, it is recorded that Cossutius undertook to design the architectur, of which no commentary has been found. And yet, not only Cossutius is to be missed in writings on these matters, but also Gaius Mucius, who, relying on great knowledge, completed the symmetry of the columns and epistyles of the temple of Honor and Virtue of Mariana, according to the legitimate rules of art. But if it had been made of marble, so that it would have authority from magnificence and expense, as well as from subtlety of art, it would have been named among the first and greatest works.

entries.latin: Cum ergo et antiqui nostri inveniantur non minus quam Graeci fuisse magni architecti et nostra memoria satis multi, et ex his pauci praecepta edidissent, non putavi silendum sed disposite singulis voluminibus de singulis exponere. rebus itaque quoniam sexto volumine privatorum aedificiorum rationes perscripsi, in hoc qui septimum tenet numerum de expolitionibus quibus rationibus et venustatem et firmitatem habere possint exponam.
entries.translation: Since, therefore, our ancients are found to have been no less great architects than the Greeks, and there are quite a few of them in our memory, and of these few have published precepts, I did not think it necessary to be silent, but to explain each one in order in each volume. Therefore, since in the sixth volume I have written down the methods of private buildings, in this, which contains the seventh volume, I will explain the refinements by which they can have both beauty and strength.

entries.latin: De septem sapientibus Thales Milesius omnium rerum principium aquam est professus, Heraclitus ignem, Magorum sacerdotes aquam et ignem, Euripides, auditor Anaxagorae, quem philosophum Athenienses scaenicum appellaverunt, aera et terram, eamque e caelestium imbrium conceptionibus inseminatam fetus gentium et omnium animalium in mundo procreavisse, et quae ex ea essent prognata, cum dissolverentur temporum necessitate coacta in eandem redire, quaeque de aere nascerentur, item in caeli regiones reverti neque interitiones recipere et dissolutione mutata in eam recidere, in qua ante fuerant, proprietatem. Pythagoras vero, Empedocles, Epicharmos aliique physici et philosophi haec principia esse quattuor proposuerunt: aerem, ignem, terram, aquam, eorumque inter se cohaerentiam naturali figuratione e generum discriminibus efficere qualitates.
entries.translation: Among the Seven Sages, Thales of Miletus held that water was the first principle of all things; Heraclitus favored fire, and the priests of the Magi both water and fire. Euripides, a pupil of Anaxagoras whom the Athenians called “the philosopher of the stage”, proposed air and earth: the latter, fertilised by rain from the heavens, brought forth human beings and other living creatures. What arose from earth would return to it when dissolved by time, while what arose from air would return to the regions of the sky, not perishing but reverting through dissolution to its former nature. Pythagoras, Empedocles, Epicharmus and other natural philosophers proposed four principles — air, fire, earth and water — whose natural combination produces different qualities.

entries.latin: Animadvertimus vero non solum nascentia ex his esse procreata, sed etiam res omnes non ali sine eorum potestate neque crescere nec tueri. Namque corpora sine spiritus redundantia non possunt habere vitam, nisi aer influens cum incremento fecerit auctus et remissiones continenter. Caloris vero si non fuerit in corpore iusta comparatio, non erit spiritus animalis neque erectio firma, cibique vires non poterunt habere coctionis temperaturam. Item si non terrestri cibo membra corporis alantur, deficient et ita a terreni principii mixtione erunt deserta.
entries.translation: We observe that the elements not only produce living things: without their power nothing can be nourished, grow or be sustained. Bodies cannot live without a sufficient supply of breath, as incoming air maintains the continual expansion and contraction of breathing. Unless the body has the proper measure of heat, it lacks vitality and strength, and food cannot be digested at the necessary temperature. Unless its members are nourished by food from the earth, they fail, deprived of the contribution of the earthly element.

entries.latin: Animalia vero si fuerint sine umoris potestate, exsanguinata et exsucata [a principiorum liquore] interarescent. Igitur divina mens, quae proprie necessaria essent gentibus, non constituit difficilia et cara, uti sunt margaritae, aurum, argentum ceteraque, quae neque corpus nec natura desiderat, sed sine quibus mortalium vita non potest esse tuta, effudit ad manum parata per omnem mundum. Itaque ex his, si quid forte defit in corpore spiritus, ad restituendum aer adsignatus id praestat. Apparatus autem ad auxilia caloris solis impetus et ignis inventus tutiorem efficit vitam. Item terrenus fructus escarum praestans copiis supervacuis desiderationibus alit et nutrit animales pascendo continenter. Aqua vero non solum potus sed infinitas usu praebendo necessitates, gratas, quod est gratuita, praestat utilitates.
entries.translation: Animals deprived of moisture would likewise lose their blood and bodily fluids and dry up. The divine mind therefore did not make the necessities of human life difficult and costly to obtain, as are pearls, gold, silver and other things that neither the body nor nature requires. Instead, it made readily available throughout the world the things without which mortal life cannot be sustained. If the body lacks breath, air restores it.
