The warmth of the Sun and the use of fire provide the heat that makes life more secure. The produce of the earth supplies abundant food, continually feeding and sustaining living creatures. Water provides not only drink but countless other necessities, and its usefulness is all the more welcome because it is freely available.

entries.latin: Ex eo etiam qui sacerdotia gerunt moribus Aegyptiorum, ostendunt omnes res e liquoris potestate consistere. Itaque cum hydria aqua ad templum aedemque casta religione refertur, tunc in terra procumbentes manibus ad caelum sublatis inventionis gratias agunt divinae benignitati.
entries.translation: Those who hold priestly office according to Egyptian custom likewise show that all things depend on the power of water. When water is brought in a hydria to a temple or sanctuary with due reverence, they prostrate themselves on the ground and raise their hands to heaven, giving thanks to divine beneficence for its discovery.

entries.latin: Nobilibus athletis, qui Olympia, Pythia Isthmia, Nemea vicissent, Graecorum maiores ita magnos honores constituerunt, uti non modo in conventu stantes cum palma et corona ferant laudes, sed etiam, cum revertantur in suas civitates cum victoria, triumphantes quadrigis in moenia et in patrias invehantur e reque publica perpetua vita constitutis vectigalibus fruantur. Cum ergo id animadvertam, admiror, quid ita non scriptoribus eidem honores etiamque maiores sint tributi, qui infinitas utilitates aevo perpetuo omnibus gentibus praestant. Id enim magis erat institui dignum, quod athletae sua corpora exercitationibus efficiunt fortiora, scriptores non solum suos sensus, sed etiam omnium, <cum> libris ad discendum et animos exacuendos praeparant praecepta.
entries.translation: The Greeks established such great honors for the noble athletes who had won Olympia, Isthmia, and Nemea, that they should not only stand in the assembly and bear praise with a palm and a crown, but also, when they returned to their cities with victory, be carried triumphantly in chariots into the walls and into their homelands, and enjoy the fruits established by the state for life. Therefore, when I observe this, I wonder why even greater honors should not be paid to writers, who have provided infinite benefits to all nations throughout all ages. For it was more worthy of being established that athletes make their bodies stronger by exercise, writers prepare not only their own senses, but also the precepts of all, <with> books for learning and sharpening the minds.

entries.latin: Quid enim Milo Crotoniates, quod fuit invictus, prodest hominibus aut ceteri, qui eo genere fuerunt victores, nisi quod, dum vixerunt ipsi, inter suos cives habuerunt nobilitatem. Pythagorae vero praecepta, Democriti, Platonis, Aristotelis ceterorumque sapientium cotidiana perpetuis industriis culta non solum suis civibus, sed etiam omnibus gentibus recentes et floridos edunt fructus. E quibus qui a teneris aetatibus doctrinarum abundantia satiantur, optimos habent sapientiae sensus, instituunt civitatibus humanitatis mores, aequa iura, leges, quibus absentibus nulla potest esse civitas incolumis.
entries.translation: For what does Milo of Croton, who was undefeated, do to men or to others who were victors of that kind, except that, while they lived, they enjoyed nobility among their citizens? But the precepts of Pythagoras, the daily cultivation of Democritus, Plato, Aristotle, and other wise men by the constant industry, bear fresh and flourishing fruits not only to their own citizens, but also to all nations. From which those who are satisfied from an early age with the abundance of learning, have the best of wise sense, and establish in their cities the morals of humanity, just rights, and laws, without which no city can be safe.

entries.latin: Cum ergo tanta munera ab scriptorum prudentia privatim publiceque fuerint hominibus praeparata, non solum arbitror palmas et coronas his tribui oportere, sed etiam decerni triumphos et inter deorum sedes eos dedicandos iudicari.
entries.translation: Therefore, since such great gifts have been prepared for men by the prudence of writers, both privately and publicly, I think that not only should palms and crowns be awarded to them, but also that triumphs should be decreed and that they should be judged by being dedicated among the seats of the gods.

entries.latin: Et primum Platonis e multis ratiocinationibus utilissimis unam, quemadmodum ab eo explicata sit, ponam. Locus aut ager paribus lateribus si erit quadratus eumque oportuerit duplicare, quod opus fuerit genere numeri, quod multiplicationibus non invenitur, eo descriptionibus linearum emendatius reperitur. Est autem eius rei haec demonstratio. Quadratus locus, qui erit longus et latus pedes denos, efficit areae pedes C. Si ergo opus fuerit eum duplicare, id est pedum CC, item e paribus lateribus facere, quaerendum erit, quam magnum latus eius quadrati fiat, ut ex eo CC pedes duplicationibus areae respondeant. Id autem numero nemo potest invenire. Namque si XIIII constituentur, erunt multiplicati pedes CXCVI, si XV, pedes CCXXV.
entries.translation: First I shall set out one of Plato’s many valuable demonstrations, as he himself expounded it. If a place or field is square, with equal sides, and it must be doubled, this cannot be achieved by any number through multiplication, but is obtained instead by the correct drawing of lines. And this is a demonstration of this. A square place, which is ten feet long and ten feet wide, makes an area of 100 feet. Therefore, if it is necessary to double it, to make it 200 feet, and also with equal sides, it will be necessary to find how large the side of its square is made, so that from it 200 feet correspond to the doublings of the area. But no one can find this numerically. For if 14 are formed, the multiplied feet will be 196, if 15, 225 feet.

entries.latin: Ergo quoniam id non explicatur numero, in eo quadrato, longo et lato pedes X quod fuerit, linea ab angulo ad angulum diagonios perducatur, uti dividantur duo trigona aequa magnitudine, singula areae pedum quinquagenûm, ad eiusque lineae diagonalis longitudinem locus quadratus paribus lateribus describatur. Ita quam magna duo trigona in minore quadrato quinquagenûm pedum linea diagonio fuerint designata, eadem magnitudine et eodem pedum numero quattuor in maiore erunt effecta. Hac ratione duplicatio grammicis rationibus ab Platone, uti schema subscriptum est in ima pagina, explicata est.
entries.translation: Since the result cannot be expressed as a whole-number measure, draw a diagonal from corner to corner of the square ten feet long and ten feet wide. This divides it into two equal triangles, each of fifty square feet. Construct a square with equal sides on the length of that diagonal. The smaller square contains two triangles of fifty square feet; the larger contains four of the same size and area. Plato thus explained the doubling by geometrical construction, as shown in the diagram drawn at the foot of the page.

entries.latin: Item Pythagoras normam sine artificis fabricationibus inventam ostendit, et quod magno labore fabri normam facientes vix ad verum perducere possunt, id rationibus et methodis emendatum ex eius praeceptis explicatur. Namque si sumantur regulae tres, e quibus una sit pedes III, altera pedes IIII, tertia pedes V, eaeque regulae inter se compositae tangant alia aliam suis cacuminibus extremis schema habentes trigoni, deformabunt normam emendatam. Ad eas autem regularum singularum longitudines si singula quadrata paribus lateribus describantur, quod erit trium latus, areae habebit pedes VIIII, quod IIII, XVI quod V erit, XXV.
entries.translation: Pythagoras also showed how to construct a right angle without relying on a craftsman’s square. His principles provide by reason and method the accuracy that craftsmen can scarcely achieve even with great labor. Take three rules, three, four and five feet long, and join their ends to form a triangle: they will define an accurate right angle. If a square is drawn on each rule, the square on the three-foot side has an area of nine square feet, that on the four-foot side sixteen, and that on the five-foot side twenty-five.

entries.latin: Ita quantum areae pedum numerum duo quadrata ex tribus pedibus longitudinis laterum et quattuor efficiunt, aeque tantum numerum reddit id unum ex quinque descriptum. Id Pythagoras cum invenisset, non dubitans a Musis se in ea inventione monitum, maximas gratias agens hostias dicitur his immolavisse. Ea autem ratio, quemadmodum in multis rebus et mensuris est utilis, etiam in aedificiis scalarum aedificationibus, uti temperatas habeant graduum librationes, est expedita.
entries.translation: The combined area of the squares on the three-foot and four-foot sides therefore equals the area of the square on the five-foot side. When Pythagoras discovered this, he believed that the Muses had guided him and is said to have offered sacrifices to them in gratitude. The same principle is useful in many calculations and measurements, and also in setting out staircases so that their steps have a convenient inclination.

entries.latin: Si enim altitudo contignationis ab summa coaxatione ad imum libramentum divisa fuerit in partes tres, erit earum quinque in scalis scaporum iusta longitudine inclinatio. ⟨quare⟩ Quam magnae fuerint inter contignationem et imum libramentum altitudinis partes tres, quattuor a perpendiculo recedant et ibi conlocentur inferiores calces scaporum. Ita si erunt temperatae; ⟨libratae⟩ et graduum ipsarum scalarum erunt conlocationes. Item eius rei erit subscripta forma.
entries.translation: For if the height of the floor from the highest point to the lowest platform is divided into three parts, five of them will be the right length of inclination in the ladders of the rungs. However great the three parts of the height between the floor and the lowest platform, four will recede from the perpendicular and there the lower steps of the rungs will be placed. Thus they will be moderate; and the placements of the steps themselves will be. Likewise the form of this matter will be as follows.

entries.latin: Archimedis vero cum multa miranda inventa et varia fuerint, ex omnibus etiam infinita sollertia id, quod exponam, videtur esse expressum. nimirum Hiero enim Syracusis auctus regia potestate, rebus bene gestis cum auream coronam votivam diis inmortalibus in quodam fano constituisset ponendam, manupretio locavit faciendam et aurum ad sacomam adpendit redemptori. Is ad tempus opus manu factum subtiliter regi adprobavit et ad sacomam pondus coronae visus est praestitisse.
entries.translation: Among Archimedes’s many remarkable inventions, the one I shall now describe seems to show extraordinary ingenuity. When Hiero had acquired royal power at Syracuse and his affairs had prospered, he decided to dedicate a golden crown to the immortal gods in a temple. He contracted for its manufacture and weighed out the gold to the craftsman on a balance. The completed work was presented to the king at the appointed time, delicately finished, and the crown appeared to match the weight of gold supplied.

entries.latin: Posteaquam indicium est factum dempto auro tantundem argenti in id coronarium opus admixtum esse, indignatus Hiero se contemptum esse neque inveniens, qua ratione id furtum reprehenderet, rogavit Archimeden, uti in se sumeret sibi de eo cogitationem. Tunc is, cum haberet eius rei curam, casu venit in balineum, ibique cum in solium descenderet, animadvertit, quantum corporis sui in eo insideret, tantum aquae extra solium effluere. idque cum eius rei rationem explicationis ostendisset, non est moratus, sed exsiluit gaudio motus de solio et nudus vadens domum ⟨uni⟩versis significabat clara voce invenisse, quod quaereret; nam currens identidem graece clamabat: εὕρηκα, εὕρηκα.
entries.translation: Later it was reported that some gold had been removed and an equal weight of silver mixed into the crown. Indignant at the deception, but unable to find a way of exposing the theft, Hiero asked Archimedes to investigate. While considering the problem, Archimedes happened to enter a bath. As he lowered himself into the tub, he noticed that the water flowing over its edge corresponded to the volume of his body submerged in it. Realizing that this suggested a way to solve the problem, he immediately leapt from the tub in delight and went home naked, proclaiming aloud that he had found what he sought. As he ran he repeatedly cried in Greek, εὕρηκα, εὕρηκα, “I have found it, I have found it”.

entries.latin: Tum vero ex eo inventionis ingressu duas fecisse dicitur massas aequo pondere, quo etiam fuerat corona, unam ex auro et alteram ex argento. Cum ita fecisset, vas amplum ad summa labra implevit aquae, in quo demisit argenteam massam. Cuius quanta magnitudo in vasum depressa est, tantum aquae effluxit. Ita exempta massa quanto minus factum fuerat, refudit sextario mensus, ut eodem modo, quo prius fuerat, ad labra aequaretur. Ita ex eo invenit, quantum pondus argenti ad certam aquae mensuram responderet.
entries.translation: Following this discovery, he is said to have made two masses equal in weight to the crown, one of gold and the other of silver. He filled a large vessel to its brim with water and lowered the silver mass into it. The water that overflowed corresponded to the volume of the immersed mass. After removing it, he measured in sextarii the water needed to restore the former level at the brim. In this way he established how a given weight of silver corresponded to a particular volume of water.

entries.latin: Cum id expertus esset, tum auream massam similiter pleno vaso demisit et ea exempta, eadem ratione mensura addita invenit ex aquae numero sextantum: minore quanto minus magno corpore eodem pondere auri massa esset quam argenti. Postea vero repleto vaso in eadem aqua ipsa corona demissa invenit plus aquae defluxisse in corona quam in aurea eodem pondere massa, et ita ex eo, quod fuerat plus aquae in corona quam in massa, ratiocinatus reprehendit argenti in auro mixtionem et manifestum furtum redemptoris.
entries.translation: He then lowered the gold mass into the full vessel and, after removing it, measured in the same way how much water was needed to refill it. The quantity was smaller: at equal weight, gold occupied less volume than silver. Finally he refilled the vessel and immersed the crown itself. More water overflowed than when the equal weight of gold had been immersed. From this greater displacement he demonstrated the mixture of silver with the gold and exposed the craftsman’s theft.

entries.latin: Transferatur mens ad Archytae Tarentini et Eratosthenis Cyrenaei cogitata; hi enim multa et grata a mathematicis rebus hominibus invenerunt. Itaque cum in ceteris inventionibus fuerint grati, in eius rei cogitationibus maxime sunt suspecti. Alius enim alia ratione explicaverunt, quod Delo imperaverat responsis Apollo, uti arae eius, quantum haberent pedum quadratorum, id duplicarentur, et ita fore uti, qui essent in ea insula, tunc religione liberarentur.
entries.translation: Let us turn to the discoveries of Archytas of Tarentum and Eratosthenes of Cyrene, who made many contributions in mathematics of benefit to humanity. Their other inventions earned them gratitude, but they are held in particular esteem for their treatment of the following problem. Each explained in a different way how to carry out Apollo’s command, given by an oracle at Delos, that his altars should be doubled in size, and how the people of the island might thus be released from their religious obligation.

entries.latin: Itaque Archytas cylindrorum descriptionibus, Eratosthenes organica mesolabi ratione idem explicaverunt. Cum haec sint tam magnis doctrinarum iucunditatibus animadversa et cogamur naturaliter inventionibus singularum rerum considerantes effectus moveri, multas res attendens admiror etiam Democriti de rerum natura volumina et eius commentarium, quod inscribitur Χειροκμήτων; †in quo etiam utebatur anulo signaretur amolcie est expertus†.
entries.translation: Archytas explained the problem by constructions involving cylinders, and Eratosthenes by the mechanical method of the mesolabe. Such achievements reveal the great pleasures of learning, and reflection on the effects of individual discoveries naturally moves us to admiration. Among many other works, I also admire Democritus’s writings on nature and his treatise entitled Χειροκμήτων. [The following clause, which refers to the use of a ring, is corrupt in the adopted Latin text and cannot be translated securely.]

entries.latin: Ergo eorum virorum cogitata non solum ad mores corrigendos, sed etiam ad omnium utilitatem perpetuo sunt praeparata, athletarum autem nobilitates brevi spatio cum suis corporibus senescunt; [itaque neque cum maxime sunt] florentes neque posteritati hi, quemadmodum sapientium cogitata hominum vitae, prodesse possunt.
entries.translation: The discoveries of these men are therefore directed not only towards improving conduct but also towards the lasting benefit of everyone. The renown of athletes, by contrast, ages quickly with their bodies. [Thus, even when at the height of their powers,] they cannot benefit posterity as the discoveries of the wise benefit human life.

entries.latin: Cum vero neque moribus neque institutis scriptorum praestantibus tribuantur honores, ipsae autem per se mentes aeris altiora prospicientes memoriarum gradibus ad caelum elatae aevo inmortali non modo sententias sed etiam figuras eorum posteris cogunt esse notas. Itaque, qui litterarum iucunditatibus instinctas habent mentes, non possunt non in suis pectoribus dedicatum habere, sicuti deorum, sic Ennii poetae simulacrum; Accii autem carminibus qui studiose delectantur, non modo verborum virtutes sed etiam figuram eius videntur secum habere praesentem esse.
entries.translation: But since honors are not bestowed on the excellent character or institution of writers, but their minds themselves, looking higher than the air, and raised to the heavens by the steps of their memories, compel posterity to know not only their opinions but also their figures. Therefore, those whose minds are innately inclined to the delights of literature cannot help but have in their hearts, as in the case of the gods, the image of the poet Ennis; while those who delight in the study of Accius' poems seem to have present with them not only the virtues of words but also his figure.

entries.latin: Item plures post nostram memoriam nascentes cum Lucretio videbuntur velut coram de rerum natura disputare, de arte vero rhetorica cum Cicerone, multi posterorum cum Varrone conferent sermonem de lingua latina, non minus etiam plures philologi cum Graecorum sapientibus multa deliberantes secretos cum his videbuntur habere sermones, et ad summam sapientium scriptorum sententiae corporibus absentibus vetustate florentes cum insunt inter consilia et disputationes, maiores habent, quam praesentium sunt, auctoritates omnes.
entries.translation: Likewise, many who were born after our memory will be seen to be discussing with Lucretius, as if in person, about the nature of things, and with Cicero, about the art of rhetoric; many of posterity will converse with Varro about the Latin language; no less will many philologists be seen to be deliberating much with the wise Greeks, having secret conversations with them; and, to sum up, the opinions of wise writers, absent from their bodies, flourishing in antiquity, when they are present in the midst of counsels and discussions, have all greater authority than those of the present.

entries.latin: Itaque, Caesar, his auctoribus fretus sensibus eorum adhibitis et consiliis ea volumina conscripsi, et prioribus septem de aedificiis, octavo de aquis, in hoc de gnomonicis rationibus, quemadmodum de radiis solis in mundo sunt per umbras gnomonis inventae quibusque rationibus dilatentur aut contrahantur, explicabo.
entries.translation: Relying on these authors, Caesar, and drawing on their ideas and counsel, I have written these books. In the first seven I treated buildings, in the eighth water, and in this one I shall explain gnomonics: how the Sun’s rays are traced through the shadows of gnomons, and by what principles those shadows lengthen or shorten.

entries.latin: Nobili Graecorum et ampla civitate Ephesi lex vetusta dicitur a maioribus dura condicione sed iure esse non iniquo constituta. Nam architectus, cum publicum opus curandum recipit, pollicetur, quanto sumptu id sit futurum. Tradita aestimatione magistratui bona eius obligantur, donec opus sit perfectum. Absoluto autem, cum ad dictum inpensa respondit, decretis et honoribus ornatur. Item si non amplius quam quarta, ad aestimationem est adicienda, de publico praestatur, neque ulla poena tenetur. Cum vero amplius quam quarta in opere consumitur, ex eius bonis ad perficiendum pecunia exigitur.
entries.translation: In the great and distinguished Greek city of Ephesus, the ancestors are said to have established an ancient law, severe in its terms yet not unjust. When an architect undertakes a public building, he declares its estimated cost. Once that estimate has been submitted to the magistrate, his property stands as security until the work is complete. If the final expenditure agrees with the estimate, he receives public honors and decrees of recognition. An overrun of no more than one quarter is covered by the public treasury without penalty. If the excess exceeds one quarter, however, the additional money required to complete the work is recovered from the architect’s own property.

entries.latin: Utinam dii inmortales fecissent, ea lex etiam <> P<> R<> non modo publicis sed etiam privatis aedificiis esset constituta! Namque non sine poena grassarentur inperiti, sed qui summa doctrinarum subtilitate essent prudentes, sine dubitatione profiterentur architecturam, neque patres familiarum inducerentur ad infinitas sumptuum profusiones, ut et e bonis eicerentur, ipsique architecti poenae timore coacti diligentius modum inpensarum ratiocinantes explicarent, uti patres familiarum ad id, quod praeparavissent, seu paulo amplius adicientes, aedificia expedirent. Nam qui quadringenta ad opus possunt parare, si adicient centum, habendo spem perfectionis delectationibus tenentur; qui autem adiectione dimidia aut ampliore sumptu onerantur, amissa spe et inpensa abiecta, fractis rebus et animis desistere coguntur.
entries.translation: Would that the gods had made immortal, that law had been established not only for public but also for private buildings among the Roman people! For the ignorant would not have been able to go about without punishment, but those who were wise in the highest subtlety of doctrines would have professed architecture without hesitation, nor would the heads of families have been led to endless profusions of expense, and so that they might be driven out of their possessions, and the architects themselves, compelled by fear of punishment, would have been more diligent in calculating the amount of expense, so that the heads of families might have prepared for what they had prepared, or by adding a little more, and would have been able to complete the buildings. For those who can prepare four hundred works, if they add a hundred, are bound by the pleasures of having the hope of perfection; but those who, by adding half, are burdened with a larger expense, are forced to desist, having lost hope and wasted their efforts, with their things and spirits broken.

entries.latin: Nec solum id vitium in aedificiis, sed etiam in muneribus, quae a magistratibus foro gladiatorum scaenisque ludorum dantur, quibus nec mora neque expectatio conceditur, sed necessitas finito tempore perficere cogit, id est sedes spectaculorum velorumque inductiones et ea omnia, quae scaenicis moribus per machinationem ad spectationes populo comparantur. In his vero opus est prudentia diligens et ingenii doctissimi cogitata, quod nihil eorum perficitur sine machinatione studiorumque vario ac sollerti vigore.
entries.translation: The same difficulty arises not only in buildings but also in the public spectacles provided by magistrates: gladiatorial displays in the forum and theatrical games. Such events admit neither postponement nor delay; seating, awnings and the apparatus required by stage practice must all be ready at a fixed time for the public to see. These undertakings demand careful judgment and highly trained ingenuity, for none can be accomplished without machinery and the varied, resourceful application of technical knowledge.

entries.latin: Igitur quoniam haec ita sunt tradita et constituta, non videtur esse alienum, uti caute summaque diligentia, antequam instituantur opera, eorum expediantur, rationes. Ergo quoniam neque lex neque morum institutio id potest cogere et quotannis et praetores et aediles ludorum causa machinationes praeparare debent, visum mihi est, imperator, non esse alienum, quoniam de aedificiis in prioribus voluminibus exposui, in hoc, quod finitionem summam corporis habet constitutam, quae sint principia machinarum, ordinata praeceptis explicare.
entries.translation: Therefore, since these things have been handed down and established in this way, it does not seem out of place that, before the works are instituted, their reasons should be carefully and diligently explained. Therefore, since neither law nor morals can compel this, and since every year both praetors and aediles must prepare machines for the games, it has seemed to me, emperor, that it is not out of place, since I have explained buildings in previous volumes, to explain, in this respect, that the finality of the body is established, what are the principles of the machines, ordered by precepts.
